title: The Order of the Silver Star
type: Fein Uaill · honor, defense and living memory
dek: Soldiers, historians and craftspeople who defend Zarathis by carrying its past into the present—and must decide what preserving it requires.

body:
The Silver Star guards people, places and the stories through which Zarathis understands itself. Its members appear at the gates and in the quarry, in libraries, at a funeral and on the floor of a leadership gathering. Its reverence for the past is practical: a maintained defense, a carefully worked stone, a record worth preserving, a duty carried through disagreement.

Compare the four factions → · All factions → · Fein Uaill →

What the Order stands for

The Order’s stated ideals are honor, defense and military tradition; its named leader is Lord-Captain Tyragol. It presents an old military order committed to justice, loyalty and the protection of the realm. Its code favors conduct that can be defended openly; secret manipulation sits uneasily with that self-image.

When Tarwen introduces himself to the visiting company, he calls the Silver Star the guardian of society against threats within and without. Structure, honor and reverence for the past belong together in his account. Later, hearing Draygar discuss his work, he offers fellowship through the Order’s ancient arcane craftsmanship. The Silver Star’s tradition includes making things well, rather than only fighting with them.

Gates, stone and the work of preservation

The Gates of Aelthor are a military outpost under Silver Star control. Travel, training and defense meet there. The Order shares military ground with the Radiant Flame, whose appetite for advance does not remove the need to guard a home behind it.

In the Month of Moirah, Year 2, Fenwae takes Olokun through teleportation circles to the mountain workings. The quarry’s laborers are well fed, its air clean; engineering and magic move the heavy marble. Fenwae values good building stone above the treasure a visitor might expect to find underground.

At a new drinking-water dam, he explains that the masons consult the Verdant Circle about the river. The promise that a continuing flow will let the ecosystem recover is their assurance, not a witnessed report from the future. His conversation with Olokun also changes tone: defending Aria gives way to hearing why the visitors felt hurt. Cultural loyalty does not prevent this working man from listening.

Tyragol, Tarwen and people who choose the Order

Tyragol welcomes Magnus home at the Niriin gathering, then resists Eldin’s attempts to draw out his stories. He calls himself an unobserved observer and deflects questions about his title. The Order’s named leader is a public presence with deliberately guarded explanations; his reserve does not establish a hidden identity or an unseen office.

Tarwen is an emissary, host and former warrior, not another name for Tyragol. Fenwae’s masonry gives the Order a further face. Among the visiting company, Wren asks to join and receives a welcome; Draygar and Eldin later speak of their Silver Star duties even while their friends leave Fein Uaill. Their commitments survive disagreement with other Zarathians. Tarwen subsequently offers Silver Star headquarters as a trusted place to receive property for a member.

Defense beside the other factions

At the lakeside readiness exercise, Silver Star and Radiant Flame generals watch the competitors. Arandiel insists that a commander who throws away soldiers will answer for it. The exercise uses Verdant Circle protection on the boats; its military purpose relies on work outside either martial order.

After Eugene wins, Arandiel describes Magnus’s near success as characteristic Silver caution. That is a rival commander’s judgment, not proof that every member fights alike. The later Void expedition complicates a simple division between cautious historians and reckless explorers: Silver Star scholars help the Emerald Veil prepare the portal while Radiant Flame warriors make up much of the fighting strength.

A keeper of history who backs Wren

After Aria’s death, Tyragol speaks as a candidate. He calls himself the keeper of Zarathis’s history and promises both to build on its past and correct its mistakes. When the factions make their nominations, however, he chooses Lady Wren.

He later explains that nominating himself would have been dishonorable. Wren, he says, most closely embodies the Order’s honor and respect. The distinction matters: a personal candidacy, a faction’s endorsement and the eventual result are separate acts. Bowene’s instruction to gather and count votes does not by itself establish who wins. The Silver Star’s choice is recorded even though its Lord-Captain does not choose himself.

Returning the dead to the earth

At the memorial in the Month of Hope, Year 2, local people explain that the Silver Star takes responsibility for returning the dead to the earth, while the Radiant Flame tends the rites preserving their spirit. Memory is part of the Order’s public service at the point where military glory ends.

The same gathering brings Elenia’s divine restoration into conflict with Zarathian custom. Magnus asks that she lose her Radiant Flame standing. His demand is an action by a Silver Star member, not a recorded vote of the whole Order or proof that the requested punishment immediately occurs. The subsequent confrontation and exile belong to Elenia’s history and Zarathis’s wider struggle over authority.

Preserving a society without freezing it

Tarwen describes the Radiant Flame as forging history while it is hot, and the Silver Star as preserving the finished work. Yet he also says his duty to Zarathis as a citizen comes before his duty to the Order if disaster threatens. His conservatism has a stated limit.

The Order’s public history therefore contains more than obedience to an inherited account. It includes craft, care for the dead, a nomination grounded in conduct and members negotiating what loyalty requires. Its complete internal hierarchy, the full reach of Tyragol’s authority and every member’s later standing remain unestablished.
